title: Social Security Design and Its Political Support
text:
The supplemental appendix
This supplemental appendix accompanies Social Security Design and Its Political Support. It extends the paper’s three quantitative sections, on Argentina’s pension reform, on the rich economies with the pension design given and on the endogenous design. It shows the results across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity, the alternative calibration of the taste for leisure, the UK’s calibration, the paths behind the paper’s readings in a single year, the corner without the cost under two timings of the choice, a second cost of redistribution, the tax rate against a pinned design and the numbers behind the paper’s decompositions of the design choice, the cross-country test under each of its variants, and the UK and France calibrated in full. Every number is built by the paper’s own pipeline from the model’s results; none is typed.

title: A. Argentina
text:
Section 5 of the paper calibrates the model with informal households to Argentina before its coverage reforms and reads the reforms as a rise of the universal pension ε; appendix E gives the household survey and the identification. This part shows how the equilibrium depends on the whole pension design, how the reform and the calibration depend on the intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES), and what changes when the taste for leisure is identified quartile by quartile.

A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria: the equilibrium in 2010 over a grid of designs (ε, θ), with the reform as a move across it.
A2. The intertemporal elasticity of substitution: the calibration and the reform’s paths in levels at each IES of the grid.
A3. Identification of X: the paper’s common taste for leisure against one per quartile.

title: A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria
text:
Each point of the figure is an economy that has always had one pension design, the universal pension ε on the horizontal axis and the design θ, the weight on earnings-related benefits, in the color, read in 2010 under log preferences; every other parameter is the paper’s calibration. A higher universal pension raises the equilibrium tax rate and lowers the savings rate, the workweek and the savings of informal relative to formal households. A more Bismarckian design lowers the tax rate and raises the savings rate and the workweek. The black line is the calibrated θ, and its two markers are the pre-reform ε and the universal level the reform installs. Between them the tax rate rises by more than the reform raises it on impact in section 5: here informal households have always saved under the universal system, while on impact the retirees of 2010 hold savings made under the old one. The rise between the markers is close to the reform’s effect in 2040, once those savings have adjusted.
\(\cdot\)

title: A2. The intertemporal elasticity of substitution
text:
Argentina’s calibration across the intertemporal elasticity
The paper’s benchmark is log preferences, and figure 3 reports the reform across the IES ρ. Each ρ is calibrated anew to the same targets, so a change of ρ moves the calibrated parameters as well as the curvature of utility. This page shows both.
Four panels are parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at each ρ, and two are predictions of the calibration, the savings rate and the informal savings ratio in 2010. The discount factor and the political weight of the old both fall as the IES rises. The second falls because the young resist taxation less, so a lighter weight of the old reproduces the observed tax rate. At the lowest elasticities of the grid the thirty-year discount factor exceeds one. The savings rate falls with the IES and the informal savings ratio rises, while the informal productivity and taste for leisure barely move.
\(\cdot\)

title: A3. Identification of X
text:
The calibration
The paper takes the taste for leisure \(X\) common to the four formal income quartiles and pins its level by the average formal workweek, so that relative hours across the quartiles are a prediction. The alternative takes the survey’s relative hours as data and identifies one \(X_i\) per quartile, which leaves the level of hours unidentified. The two calibrations share their targets, \(\beta\), \(\omega\) and every equilibrium outcome of section 5: the tax rate, savings, hours in efficiency units and the reform at every ρ. The reason is that the productivity distribution reaches the aggregates only through \(\sum_{i>0}\gamma_i\eta_i^{1+\xi}/X_i^{\xi}\), which both calibrations normalize to one (appendix E). The tables below therefore show only what differs.
Four rows of the paper’s calibration table differ. In the survey, hours rise less with income than the common \(X\) predicts: the top quartile works fewer hours than predicted, and the others a little more. The vector \(X_i\) take those hours as data, so the taste for leisure rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart to reproduce the same relative incomes. The informal productivity and taste for leisure are measured against the formal average and move with it.
\(\cdot\)

title: A3. Identification of X
text:
Why the level of \(X\) differs
The level of the taste for leisure is not comparable across the two calibrations. Under the common \(X\) it is the unit in which hours are measured: it is set so that average formal hours in the model equal the observed workweek, and every productivity scales with it. Under the vector \(X_i\) the survey’s relative hours fix only the ratios of the \(X_i\), and the unit of hours is a normalization, which sets the level of every \(X_i\), of the productivities and of the informal taste for leisure. Since that level enters no aggregate, nothing else moves. Across the IES, the common \(X\) falls a little as ρ rises, because average hours are matched against a slightly different equilibrium at each ρ, while the informal parameters barely move under either calibration.

title: B. Rich OECD countries with the design given
text:
Section 6 of the paper calibrates the model without informal households to the U.S. and France and changes the U.S. calibration one characteristic at a time: its pension design, its demography, and the income distribution, voting patterns and taste for leisure that set France apart. Appendix F gives the data and the household heterogeneity of the two. This part shows the calibrations of the U.S., the UK and France across the IES, the U.S. counterfactuals across the Frisch elasticity and the tax rate against inherited savings, what changes when the taste for leisure is identified group by group, and the UK’s calibration, which the deep test of C5 uses.

B1. Calibration: the three calibrations at every IES of the grid.
B2. Other parameters: the U.S. counterfactuals across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity, and the tax rate against inherited savings.
B3. Identification of X: the common taste for leisure against one per income group.
B4. The UK: the three calibrations side by side and the UK’s income groups.

title: B1. Calibration
text:
The calibrations across the intertemporal elasticity
Each country is calibrated at every ρ of the grid against its own targets. The discount factor is calibrated on the U.S. and imposed on the UK and France, so their interest factors are predictions. The political weight of the old falls as the IES rises in every country, since the young resist taxation less, and it keeps its ranking: highest in France, then the U.S., lowest in the UK. The savings rate falls with the IES in every country, and the UK’s and France’s interest factors rise toward the U.S. target. The taste for leisure, pinned by each country’s average workweek, falls a little with the IES in the UK and is nearly flat in the U.S. and France. At the lowest elasticity of the grid the thirty-year discount factor exceeds one, which the UK and France inherit.
\(\cdot\)

title: B2. Other parameters
text:
The U.S. across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity
The figure shows the counterfactuals of section 6 on the U.S. across the two elasticities that govern the households’ responses. The intertemporal elasticity ρ varies at the paper’s Frisch elasticity; the Frisch elasticity ξ varies under log preferences. At each ξ the U.S. and France are recalibrated to the same targets, so the discount factor, the political weight of the old and the taste for leisure take new values. The ranking of the determinants holds at every ξ of the grid: ageing and the design move the tax rate most, France’s characteristics far less. A higher Frisch elasticity dampens the responses of the tax rate a little and some responses of savings by more, and it enlarges the responses of hours, since labor supply is more elastic, all but that to France’s taste for leisure, which it makes a little smaller.

title: B2. Other parameters
section: The tax rate and inherited savings
text:
The tax rate and inherited savings
The tax rate of the Markov equilibrium is a function of the state the economy inherits, the savings of the previous period’s young. The figure shows the U.S. tax policy of 2020 at inherited savings below and above their value on the equilibrium path, each IES at its own calibration. Under log preferences the tax rate does not depend on the state (section 3). Away from log preferences it does: at an IES of one half the tax rate falls as inherited savings rise, and at an IES of two it rises, less steeply.
\(\cdot\)

title: B3. Identification of X
text:
The calibration
As for Argentina (A3), the paper takes the taste for leisure \(X\) common to the income groups and pins its level by each country’s average workweek; the alternative identifies one \(X_i\) per group from the observed relative hours. In every country the two calibrations share the discount factor, the political weight of the old, the tax rate, savings and aggregate hours. They also share every counterfactual that changes neither the productivities nor the taste for leisure: the design, ageing and France’s voting patterns. The tables and the figure show only what differs.
Two rows of the paper’s calibration table differ, the taste for leisure and the productivity spread. Under the vector \(X_i\) the taste for leisure rises with income in all three countries: observed hours rise less with income than the common \(X\) predicts, the high group working fewer hours than predicted. To reproduce the same relative incomes with those hours, the productivity spread widens.
\(\cdot\)
Group by group, the vector \(X_i\) are a fraction of the common \(X\), and their level carries no information of its own. Under the common \(X\) the level is the unit of hours: it is set so that the model’s average workweek is the observed one, relative to the U.S. for the UK and France, and the productivities scale with it. Under the vector \(X_i\) the relative hours fix only the ratios of the \(X_i\), and the unit is a normalization. That is why the level differs so much between the two while every aggregate is the same.
\(\cdot\)

title: B4. The UK
text:
The UK is calibrated as the U.S. and France are in appendix F of the paper, under log preferences, to its own pension spending, demography, design and average workweek, with the U.S. discount factor imposed. Its household data are the Harmonised British Household Panel Survey, wave 17, which refers to 2006–07 and is distributed by the UK Data Service; later waves were collected at least in part during the Great Recession. The income groups are cut as for the U.S., so that the mean incomes of the low and medium groups are half the mean and the mean. The cuts set the population shares and the productivities, not the design: θ is the slope of the public pension on earnings, measured as for every country of the paper’s cross-country test (appendix G.1 of the paper). The propensities to vote are from the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES). B1 gives the calibration at every IES of the grid, and C5 lets the UK’s electorate choose its design.
Table B4.1 sets the UK beside the U.S. and France. Its design is the least Bismarckian of the three, and its population is older than the U.S. one and younger than France’s. Its tax rate is a little above the U.S. one, while its calibrated political weight of the old is the lowest of the three: in the model an older population and flatter benefits both raise the tax rate the electorate chooses at a given weight (section 3 of the paper). The ratio of high to low productivity is close to the U.S. one and well above France’s. The common taste for leisure, pinned by the UK’s average workweek relative to the U.S. one, is the highest of the three, almost twice the U.S. level.

title: C. Endogenous design
text:
Section 7 of the paper lets the electorate choose the design θ as well as the tax rate, under a deadweight cost of redistribution whose parameter λ is calibrated so that the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design. Appendix C.2 sets out the steps behind the cost, a reduced form whose size is left to the calibration. This part follows the design along each country’s projected demography; reports the corner the design reaches without the cost under two timings of the choice, sets a second cost specification against the paper’s and the tax rate against a pinned design, and gives the numbers behind the paper’s decompositions of the design choice; varies the elasticities; shows the cross-country test under each of its variants in full; and calibrates the UK and France in full.

C1. The path in levels: the design, the tax rate, savings and hours as the U.S., the UK and France age, with the design chosen and with it pinned.
C2. The cost of redistribution: the corner the design reaches without the cost, chosen with the tax and one period ahead; the paper’s cost against a cost attached to the design itself, both calibrated; the U.S. tax rate against a pinned design, with and without the cost; and the numbers behind the paper’s decompositions of the design choice and of the size of the cost.
C3. Other parameters: the U.S. across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity.
C4. The cross-country test: the test of section 7.3 under each variant of appendix G in full, with Luxembourg left out and with the model at the U.S. political weight.
C5. The UK and France calibrated in full: the deep test under the U.S. cost parameter, each country’s own parameter, and the UK’s at every IES.

title: C1. The path in levels
text:
By country
The calibration targets the design of 2020 only; every other design along the path is an outcome of the model, chosen one period ahead. The first two figures follow the three countries from 1990, whose electorate sets the design of 2020, to 2110; the demography is constant from 2080. Each country keeps its own calibration and demography. Its cost parameter is either the U.S. λ, the deep test of C5 along the path, or its own, the parameter at which its electorate re-elects its observed design.
In every country the chosen design moves against the number of workers per retiree. As the population ages, the electorate ties benefits more closely to earnings, and the design levels off when the demography does. Under the U.S. cost parameter France’s design stays above the U.S. one, but from 2050 by much less, since France’s population is already old in 2020 and ages least afterwards. The UK’s design lies above the U.S. one until 2020, only slightly in 2020, and below it from 2050, so that from then on the three designs keep their observed order, the UK’s lowest and France’s highest. The UK’s workers per retiree rise until 2020 before they fall, and its design moves against them, falling and then rising. At their own parameters the UK’s and France’s designs pass through their observed values in 2020 and follow the same patterns. The tax rate rises with ageing everywhere.

title: C2. The cost of redistribution
text:
Without the cost: the corner
Section 7.1 of the paper adds a deadweight cost of redistribution because without one the electorate chooses flat benefits. This page shows that corner first, under the two timings of the choice the paper examines, then sets a second specification of the cost against the paper’s and reads the U.S. tax rate against a pinned design, and closes with the numbers behind the paper’s decompositions of the design choice and of the size of the cost.
Appendix C.1 of the paper shows that, without the cost of redistribution and at the U.S. calibration, each of the two timings it examines puts the design at the Beveridgean corner. A design chosen together with the tax rate re-splits benefits that current retirees have already earned, and under log preferences a more earnings-related one lowers the political objective as long as the propensity to vote rises with income by proportionally less than consumption in retirement. A design chosen one period ahead weighs the young’s stake in redistribution against the gain of a more earnings-related system, which raises the labor supply on which benefits are levied.
Table C2.1 reports the numerical checks, one block per timing. Chosen with the tax, the design’s marginal effect on the political objective is negative at every date and every design at each IES, so the design is the Beveridgean corner. The corner would fail only if the weight of the high-income group relative to the low-income one exceeded a critical ratio, which is above the observed ratio at every IES and every date. The critical ratio falls as the IES rises, and along the projection as the system grows; at its lowest, at the highest IES late in the projection, it remains above the observed ratio. Chosen one period ahead under log preferences, the design is again the Beveridgean corner.

title: C2. The cost of redistribution
text:
A cost on the design
Under the paper’s cost of redistribution, which lifts the design off that corner, the share of revenue lost grows with the square of the size of the system and with the dispersion of relative incomes, so nothing is lost when the design redistributes nothing (appendix C.2). The alternative attaches the cost to the design itself, \(f(\theta) = \phi + (1-\phi)\theta^{p}\), with \(\phi\) imposed and \(p\) calibrated, as λ is, so that the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design. It charges a flat benefit whatever that benefit redistributes. Table C2.2 gives the two calibrations under log preferences, the only IES at which the cost on the design is calibrated. At the observed design the cost on the design loses a larger share of revenue than the paper’s, and at a flat benefit it loses the share \(1-\phi\), far more.

section: The tax against a pinned design
text:
The tax against a pinned design
The figure pins the U.S. design at one value on the whole path, with the calibration held at the observed design, and reads the tax rate of 2020 without the cost of redistribution and with the paper’s cost. Both lines pass through the calibrated tax rate at the observed design. Without the cost the tax rate falls as the design becomes more Bismarckian, the comparative static of section 3 of the paper: a higher θ shifts benefits from low-income retirees, who with their higher marginal utility weigh more in the political objective, to high-income ones. With the cost the tax rate is hump-shaped in the design, with its peak a little above the observed design, which the electorate re-elects. At flatter designs a more Bismarckian one raises the tax rate, since less of the revenue is lost; at more Bismarckian designs it lowers the tax rate, as without the cost. Section 7 of the paper opens with this shape.

section: The numbers behind the paper’s decompositions
text:
The numbers behind the paper’s decompositions
Table C2.3 gives the numbers behind three statements the paper makes in words. Panel A splits the design condition of the U.S. electorate under log preferences at the design it chooses (section 7.1): with the share of revenue lost and the anticipated tax held, the political objective pulls the design towards flat benefits, and two routes offset that pull in nearly equal parts, the saving on the loss, since a more earnings-related design dissipates less of the revenue that pays the young, and the response of the anticipated tax. Panel B imposes France’s income distribution on the U.S. in three steps (section 7.2): first everywhere but in the cost, then in the dispersion of relative incomes in the cost, and last in the tax rate in the cost. The first step raises the design at each IES, most at the highest; the other two lower it, and the dispersion in the cost lowers it most at the lowest IES, where λ is largest. The split depends on the order of the steps, and the last row imposes the dispersion in the cost alone. Panel C sets the calibrated λ against the participation and taxable-income elasticities of the literature (appendix C.2): through the local elasticity of the base at the wedge in place, λ is a multiple of what those elasticities imply at each IES, a multiple that falls as the IES rises. Charging the budget with the fiscal externality of the response instead scales the loss up, so that the calibrated λ implies a smaller elasticity and a smaller share of earnings outside the base.

title: C4. The cross-country test
text:
The paper’s specification
Section 7.3 of the paper tests the model on the countries of figure 1. Every country keeps its own workers per retiree, corrected for its gap to the U.S. in the normal retirement age, its income distribution in three groups cut at the U.S. income percentiles (appendix G.1 of the paper), its observed design and its propensities to vote by income group, from the CSES; Luxembourg, which has no CSES survey and enforces compulsory voting, votes at the same rate in every income group. Every country takes from the U.S. the discount factor \(\beta\) and the cost of redistribution as \(\kappa\), the slope of the elasticity in appendix C.2 of the paper, so that country \(n\) faces \(\lambda_{n,t} = 2\kappa\,\pi_{n,t}(1-\pi_{n,t})\) at its own ratio \(\pi_{n,t} = \Pi_{n,t}/R_{n,t}\) of the pay-as-you-go return to the market return. Every country’s ratio lies close to one half, where \(\pi(1-\pi)\) hardly moves, so that in 2020 every country’s λ lies close to the U.S. one. In the model every country also takes the same political weight of the old \(\omega\), the mean of the weights that match each country’s pension spending at its observed design; the model with each country’s own political weight, own \(\omega\) for short, calibrates each country’s \(\omega\) to that spending. The U.S. anchor, where \(\omega\) and \(\kappa\) are calibrated, is measured as every other country is (appendix G.2 of the paper). This page repeats the test under other population data and other measures of the design, without Luxembourg, and with every country in the model at the U.S. political weight.
The paper reports the test in figure 7 and table 5, the predicted against the observed designs in figure 8, and each country’s own political weight and the design it chooses with own \(\omega\) in table 10. Table C4.1 sets the paper’s test beside its variants, one column per relation of figure 1 of the paper. Its starred rows are the paper’s specification: the data and the model are those of table 5 of the paper, and with own \(\omega\) the predicted designs keep the signs of the relations that are significant in the data, and their slopes on inequality, like the data’s, are insignificant. Panel A changes the population data and panel B the measure of the design, each taken in turn below.

title: C4. The cross-country test
text:
Other population data
Panel A of table C4.1 leaves workers per retiree uncorrected for the retirement age, or corrects them for each country’s gap to the U.S. in the effective age of labor-market exit in place of the normal retirement age (OECD 2021, fig. 6.14). The data side of the test does not depend on them. With own \(\omega\) the test is hardly affected, since the political weights are calibrated to spending: no slope changes by more than 0.01, and the correlation between predicted and observed designs stays at 0.78 (figure C4.1). The model keeps the signs of the three relations that are significant in the data, and its slopes on inequality stay insignificant, but its predicted designs move more. At the exit age the correlation is 0.69, against 0.75 at the normal age. Uncorrected, it falls to 0.39, because of Luxembourg.
Luxembourg’s population grew to 1.65 times its 1990 size by 2020. At that variant’s mean political weight, 1.33, this supports a tax of only 5.5% at its observed design, about two fifths of the 12.9% its spending implies, and its electorate of 1990 chooses the Beveridgean corner for 2020, against the observed 0.820. Luxembourg’s normal retirement age is four years below the U.S. one, and the correction brings its workers per retiree in 2020 to 1.17 and its predicted design to 0.600. Without Luxembourg, on the 20 countries with a CSES survey, the correlation in the model is 0.73 with workers per retiree uncorrected, between the 0.69 of the exit age and the 0.77 of the normal age on the same countries (the last rows of panel A, and Luxembourg left out below).

title: C4. The cross-country test
text:
Other measures of the design
Panel B of table C4.1 changes the measure of the design. Each measure is its own cross-section: the data and the model are calibrated to it, on the countries where it is defined, at the paper’s population data, with the U.S. anchor recalibrated under it. The public tier on 23 countries extends the paper’s measure, the public tier, to every country whose public pension is not tested against funded tiers, which adds the Netherlands and Switzerland. All mandatory tiers takes the slope over all mandatory and quasi-mandatory tiers, public and funded (OECD 2021, table 4.1), with the same correction for top-ups, adds the spending of the funded tiers to the tax and covers all 26 countries in which informal employment is below a quarter of employment.
The public tier on 23 countries leaves the test as it is, with correlations between predicted and observed designs of 0.73 in the model and 0.79 with own \(\omega\) (figure C4.4). All mandatory tiers keeps the signs of the significant slopes. Its data add both the funded tiers and the five countries where they are large or the public pension is tested against them; in these data the slope of the index on population growth is −0.38, against −0.44 under the paper’s measure, while its slope on high over low income nearly vanishes, 0.003 against 0.076. The model predicts the design less well, with a correlation of 0.40, partly because of two countries that only this measure covers: Iceland, which the model puts at the Beveridgean corner against an observed 0.813, and Australia, which it puts at 0.072 against 0.587. Without Iceland the correlation is 0.56, and without both 0.68. With own \(\omega\), where Iceland’s political weight is calibrated to its spending, its design is 0.592 and the correlation is 0.69.

title: C5. The UK and France calibrated in full
text:
The design under the U.S. cost
Besides the U.S., the UK and France are the countries of the paper’s cross-country test with the household data to calibrate the model in full: France in appendix F of the paper, the UK in B4. Each is calibrated under log preferences to its own pension spending, demography and design, with its own propensities to vote, the UK’s households grouped at its own income cuts and France’s at the U.S. income percentiles. This deep test gives each country the U.S. cost parameter λ (table 4 of the paper), recalibrates its political weight of the old under that cost and reads the design its electorate chooses for 2020. It also calibrates each country’s own λ, the value at which its electorate re-elects its observed design.
The cross-country test carries the cost in another form, as \(\kappa\), the slope of the elasticity in appendix C.2 of the paper, which gives country \(n\) the parameter \(\lambda_{n,t} = 2\kappa\,\pi_{n,t}(1-\pi_{n,t})\) at its own ratio \(\pi_{n,t} = \Pi_{n,t}/R_{n,t}\) of the pay-as-you-go return to the market return. With \(\kappa\) calibrated on the U.S., as λ is, the parameter this gives the UK and France in 2020 lies close to the U.S. λ, the UK’s a little above it and France’s a little below it. France’s ratio is well below the U.S. one and the UK’s a little below it, but all three lie close to one half, where \(\pi(1-\pi)\) hardly moves. The two forms in which the cost can be carried to another economy therefore nearly coincide.
Under the U.S. λ France’s electorate chooses a design just below its observed one, and the UK’s a design far above its own and slightly above the U.S. one. The U.S. parameter thus reproduces nearly all of the distance by which France’s design exceeds the U.S. one and none of the distance by which the UK’s falls short of it: France’s design stays the highest of the three, as observed, while the UK’s moves from the lowest to just above the U.S. one. The own parameters rank as the observed designs do, the UK’s at about half the U.S. value and France’s about a tenth above it. A higher parameter, under which flat benefits lose more revenue, moves the design away from the Beveridgean corner: the U.S. λ is above the UK’s own and below France’s, and it raises the UK’s design and lowers France’s.
\(\cdot\)

title: D1. The OECD cross-section
text:
Inequality: the Gini and the model’s measures
Figure 1 of the paper sets pension spending and the Bismarckian index of the OECD countries against their population growth and their income inequality. The countries are the OECD members before 2000 in which informal employment is low and one public pay-as-you-go system pays the bulk of retirement benefits. The index is \(I = 1/(2-\theta)\) of the design θ: the earnings-linked share of the least-squares line through the public pension across earnings levels, for men under the rules of 2020 (Pensions at a Glance 2021), times one minus the share of public pension spending on minimum top-ups and tested benefits. Appendix G.1 of the paper gives the rule and the measure. The cross-country test of section 7.3 runs on the same countries, Luxembourg, which has no CSES survey of the propensities to vote, at a flat profile (C4). The tabs below the figure give the values behind each marker with the year each refers to, the provider, dataset and series of every column with the date it was retrieved, and the pairwise correlations the paper’s introduction describes.
\(\cdot\)
The paper measures income inequality as the model does. Each synthetic country of sections 6 and 7 carries three income groups, at the U.S. shares of the population, with the relative earnings \(y_i\) of its men in full-time work, and the paper’s measure is high over low income, \(y_3/y_1\), the relative earnings of the top group over those of the bottom one. The model’s own summary of the same groups is the dispersion \(\tilde V = \sum_i \gamma_i (y_i - 1)^2/y_i\), which scales the share of revenue lost to the cost of redistribution in section 7. A more common measure is the Gini coefficient of disposable income, which covers all households and all incomes, and counts income after taxes and transfers, public pensions among them.
Figure D1.2 sets the two model-based measures against the Gini, and table D1.4 gives their correlations. Figure D1.3 and table D1.5 redraw the inequality panels of figure 7 of the paper under each of the three measures, with the data and the model of the paper’s specification. The paper’s conclusion does not depend on the measure: under none of them is spending or the Bismarckian index significantly related to inequality, in the data or in the model.

title: D2. Numerical checks
text:
The horizon and the terminal condition
Section 4 of the paper computes date-specific Markov policy functions by backward induction along the demographic transition, and tests every candidate equilibrium at each state; the technical documentation (Berg and Gonzalez-Eiras 2026) gives the algorithms. The first table compares the date-specific solution with a time-invariant policy function, the approximation of much of the quantitative politico-economic literature, at the same dates. The second counts, by the solves that wrote them, and the third, for every file of results that records them, the equilibria and the candidates found at any state, and the states at which no candidate passed the test; appendix D of the paper states these counts for the paper’s results. There the solver falls back on a rule of the technical documentation: it ranks the candidate taxes by the integral of the first order condition, and the designs by the political objective with each design at its own consistent distribution of savings. The tables record a fallback only in the choice of the design. A single equilibrium at every state means that the selection rule of section 4 never had to choose.
Appendix D of the paper solves the calibrated economies again with the backward induction started two periods earlier, three periods later and under its steady-state terminal condition, and reports the outcomes in the calibration year and one period later. The table gives the change against the paper’s horizon at every date to the last dated period. Under log preferences the U.S. outcomes do not depend on the horizon. Elsewhere a longer horizon or the steady-state terminal condition moves the tax rate by a few hundredths of a percentage point at most at any date, and the chosen design by less than a thousandth. A horizon two periods shorter moves the outcomes of the calibration year as little, but those of the last dated periods by more, since its terminal period is then close. At the paper’s horizon every date it reports is within a few hundredths of a percentage point of its value under the steady-state terminal condition.
